summary: The binary, denary and hexadecimal number systems, converting between them, why hexadecimal is used in computer systems, and adding and multiplying binary numbers, including overflow.

blocks.content: Computers store and process **all data as binary** — patterns of **0s and 1s** — because their circuits have two states (on/off). People normally use **denary** (decimal), and programmers often use **hexadecimal** as a short way to write binary.

items.title: Units
items.content:
- **Bit** — one binary digit, 0 or 1.
- **Nibble** — 4 bits (one hexadecimal digit).
- **Byte** — 8 bits; values 0–255 (00000000–11111111, 00–FF).

items.title: How many values?
items.content:
- *n* bits can store **2ⁿ** different values: 4 bits → 16, 8 bits → 256, 16 bits → 65 536.
- The largest unsigned number in *n* bits is **2ⁿ − 1**: 8 bits → 255.

blocks.title: Place values of an 8-bit binary number
Binary → denary
items: Write the **place values** (128, 64, 32 … 1) above the bits.
**Add** the place values where the bit is **1**.

blocks.title: Denary → binary (place-value method)
items: Start with the largest place value (128). If it fits into the number, write **1** and **subtract** it; otherwise write **0**.

blocks.title: Denary → binary (division method)
items: **Divide by 2** repeatedly and write down the **remainders**.
Read the remainders from the **bottom up**.

blocks.title: Binary → hexadecimal
items: Split the binary number into groups of **4 bits (nibbles)** from the **right**; add leading 0s if needed.
Convert each nibble to **one hex digit** (8-4-2-1 place values).

blocks.title: Hexadecimal → binary
items: Convert **each hex digit** into **4 bits**.

blocks.title: Hexadecimal ↔ denary
items: **Hex → denary:** multiply each digit by its place value (16, 1) and add. *7A* = 7 × 16 + 10 = **122**.
**Denary → hex:** divide by 16; the quotient is the first digit, the remainder the second. *245* = 15 × 16 + 5 → **F5**.

items.title: Advantages of hexadecimal
items.content:
- **Shorter** than binary — one hex digit replaces **4 bits**, so a byte is just **2 digits** (B6 instead of 10110110).
- **Easier for people to read, write and remember** than long binary strings.
- **Fewer mistakes** when copying or typing values.
- **Easy to convert** to and from binary (each digit = one nibble), unlike denary.
- The computer still works in **binary** — hex is only for **people**.

items.title: Where hexadecimal is used
items.content:
- **Colour codes** in HTML/CSS: `#FF0000` (red), `#1F4FD8`.
- **MAC addresses**: `00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E`.
- **Memory addresses** and **machine code** in debuggers and assembly.
- **Error codes** (e.g. Windows `0x0000007B`) and **IPv6** addresses.
- Representing **Unicode** characters (U+0041 = "A").

blocks.title: Reading an HTML colour code
blocks.content: `#2E8B57` → red **2E** = 46, green **8B** = 139, blue **57** = 87. Each pair is **one byte** (0–255) for one colour channel.

blocks.title: Checking the answer
items: Convert both numbers and the answer to **denary**: 109 + 54 = 163 ✔.

blocks.content: An **overflow error** occurs when the result of a calculation is **too large to fit** in the number of bits available. In 8 bits the largest value is **255**, so a result of 256 or more needs a **9th bit**, which is lost.
The correct answer is **300**, but only **44** is stored — the leftmost carry is lost. The processor sets an **overflow flag** so the error can be detected.

blocks.title: Multiplying binary numbers (shift and add)
items: Multiply the first number by **each bit** of the second number, starting from the right: ×1 copies the number, ×0 gives zeros.
**Shift** each row one place **left** (add a 0 on the right) for each new bit.
**Add** the rows using binary addition.

blocks.content: Shifting a binary number **one place left** multiplies it by **2**; two places by 4; three places by 8. *Example:* 0011 (3) → 0110 (6) → 1100 (12). Shifting **right** divides by 2 (the remainder is lost).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Convert the denary number 200 into binary and hexadecimal. [2]**
200 = 128 + 64 + 8 → **11001000** (1); 1100 = C, 1000 = 8 → **C8** (1).

**Q: Explain two advantages of using hexadecimal in computer systems. [2]**
It is **shorter** than binary, so it is **easier for humans to read and remember** (1); it is **easy to convert** to binary because each digit represents **4 bits**, so there are **fewer errors** (1).

**Q: Add 01010110 and 00101101 and state the denary answer. [2]**
**10000011** (1) = **131** (1).

**Q: Explain what happens when 10010110 and 01111000 are added in an 8-bit register. [2]**
The result 270 is greater than **255**, so **overflow** occurs (1); only **00001110** (14) is stored / the 9th bit is lost (1).

- Reading the remainders of the division method from **top to bottom** (they are read **bottom up**).
- Splitting binary into nibbles from the **left** when the number of bits is not a multiple of 4 — always start from the **right**.
- Writing hex digits above 9 as "10", "11" — use **A–F**.
- Forgetting the **carry** in binary addition.
- Saying the computer works in hexadecimal — it works in **binary**; hex is for **humans**.

questions.title: Explain the difference

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Binary is base 2, uses digits 0 and 1 (1)
- Hexadecimal is base 16, uses 0–9 and A–F; one hex digit represents 4 binary digits (1)
scheme.model_answer: Binary is base 2 and uses only 0 and 1, whereas hexadecimal is base 16 and uses 0–9 and A–F, so one hex digit stands for 4 bits.

questions.title: Overflow
questions.text: Adding 11110000 and 00011111 in an 8-bit register causes an overflow.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: 240 + 31 = 271, which is more than 255, so a ninth bit is needed.

questions.title: Explain overflow
questions.text: Explain what is meant by an **overflow error** in binary addition, using an 8-bit register as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The result is too large to fit in the available bits — greater than 255 for 8 bits (1)
- the extra (9th) bit / carry is lost, so the stored result is wrong (1)
scheme.model_answer: An overflow happens when the answer is bigger than 255, the largest 8-bit number, so the ninth bit cannot be stored and the result kept in the register is wrong.
